profile.campus_mw_context: The 128,715-sq. ft. data center in Sterling, VA, offers 11 MW of IT capacity and features robust connectivity options with high bandwidth and high-availability circuits and a number of metro and long-haul networks.

reading.body:
CyrusOne NVA4 in Sterling, Virginia publishes 11 MW of IT capacity across 128,715 square feet, which is a mid-sized facility, not a frontier-scale one.

The pattern here is disclosure, not size. Virginia has 330 mapped data centers, but only 25 publish capacity figures, totaling 1,603 MW. This campus ranks 26th among Virginia facilities with published capacity and represents less than 1% of the state's disclosed capacity. The 11 MW figure is an IT load, the power delivered to servers, not the total power the campus draws including cooling and losses, so the grid burden is larger than the number shown.

For AI specifically, 11 MW at a common 40 kW per rack training density works out to roughly 275 racks. That is enough for enterprise workloads, specialized compute, or distributed inference, and the facility's multiple metro and long-haul circuits suit workloads where data movement matters more than raw power density. It is not a plausible site for large-scale training runs or frontier model development.

What the data does not cover is the majority of the state. With 305 Virginia facilities unmapped or unpublished, the true aggregate capacity is unknown, and this campus's rank of 26th is a rank among the disclosed minority only. Whether Sterling matters to AI scaling depends on capacity that is not in this record.
